import Presentation from "../../components/Presentation.astro"; import Slide from "../../components/Slide.astro"; import Stereogram from "../../components/Stereogram.astro"; import AutoStereogram from "../../components/AutoStereogram.astro"; import PlyVideo from "../../components/PlyVideo.astro"; # Explicit Flows for Implicit Surfaces ### Camille Buonomo Julie Digne · Raphaëlle Chaine CNRS · Université Lyon 1 · INSA Lyon # Sterrogram # Auto-Sterrogram # Shape deformation We want to deform a shape continuously: $$ \mathcal{S}_0 \longrightarrow \mathcal{S}(t) \longrightarrow \mathcal{S}_1 $$ Applications: - Shape morphing - Landmark-constrained deformation - Shape editing - Pairwise-to-any morphing # Our goal We want a deformation that is: - **continuous in time** - **invertible** - **explicitly evaluable** - valid at arbitrary positions and times - compatible with implicit representations Most importantly: > No numerical integration during inference. # Applications Interpolation · Pairwise-to-any · Shape editing # Why not directly learn a deformation? A direct mapping $$ D : \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d $$ can map the source shape to the target shape. But it does not tell us: $$ \text{What happens between } t=0 \text{ and } t=1? $$ We need a continuous trajectory for every point. # Mathematical flows A mapping $$ \phi : \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d $$ is a flow if: $$ \phi(x,0)=x $$ and $$ \phi(x,t+s) = \phi(\phi(x,s),t) $$ This second property is the **group law**. # Consequences The group law gives us: $$ \phi^{-1}(x,t)=\phi(x,-t) $$ Therefore: - trajectories cannot cross - the deformation is invertible - forward and backward motion are consistent - arbitrary time intervals can be composed # The non-stationary problem Some deformations cannot be represented as flows in the original space. Trajectories can cross in space at different times. # Lift time into the space We instead work in space-time: $$ \phi : \mathbb{R}^{d+1} \times \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{d+1} $$ with $$ \phi((x_0,t_0),t) = (x(t+t_0),t+t_0) $$ Time becomes an additional coordinate. # Implicit shape deformation Let the initial shape be represented by: $$ \mathcal{S}_0 = \{x \mid g(x)=0\} $$ We want an implicit function: $$ f(x,t) $$ representing the shape at every time. # Transporting the implicit function Level sets must be preserved: $$ f( \phi((x_0,0),t), t ) = g(x_0) $$ Using the inverse flow: $$ f(x,t) = g( \phi((x,t),-t) ) $$ So the flow directly transports the implicit representation. # Our main idea Instead of learning a vector field and integrating: $$ \dot{x}=V(x,t) $$ we directly construct: $$ \boxed{ \phi((x_0,t_0),t) = ( \psi_{t+t_0} \circ \psi_{t_0}^{-1}(x_0), t+t_0 ) } $$ where each $$ \psi_t $$ is a diffeomorphism. # Why does this work? At zero time: $$ \phi((x_0,t_0),0) = (x_0,t_0) $$ And composition gives: $$ \phi( \phi((x_0,t_0),s), t ) = \phi((x_0,t_0),s+t) $$ Therefore: $$ \boxed{\phi \text{ is a mathematical flow}} $$ # Time-parameterized diffeomorphisms We construct a family: $$ (\psi_t)_t $$ such that every: $$ \psi_t : \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^d $$ is invertible. We use a RealNVP-like architecture. # Time-parameterized coupling layers The inverse has essentially the same computational cost as the forward pass. # Coupling layer Split: $$ x=(x_I,x_{\bar I}) $$ and transform only part of the coordinates: $$ \tilde{\psi}_t(x) = \begin{pmatrix} x_I \\ s_\theta(x_I,t) \odot x_{\bar I} + v_\theta(x_I,t) \end{pmatrix} $$ # Exact inverse Because the scaling is non-zero: $$ s_\theta(x_I,t) > 0 $$ the layer is analytically invertible. Therefore: $$ \psi_t^{-1} $$ is available directly. No fixed-point iterations. No ODE solver. # EFIS ## Explicit Flow for Implicit Surfaces Our architecture gives: $$ \boxed{ \text{Flow} = \psi_{t+t_0} \circ \psi_{t_0}^{-1} } $$ Properties: - Explicit - Invertible - Continuous - Satisfies the group law - Efficient forward and inverse evaluation # Optimization We optimize the flow using: ### Endpoint constraints - Dirichlet loss - Neumann loss - Interior/exterior loss - Landmark loss ### Intermediate-time regularization - Isometry - Volume preservation - Temporal regularization # Dirichlet loss Surface points should reach the target surface: $$ g_1( \phi((x,0),1) ) = 0 $$ and backward: $$ g_0( \phi((y,1),-1) ) = 0 $$ This constrains the endpoints of the deformation. # Neumann loss We also align normals. This encourages: - smooth surfaces - consistent local geometry - better intermediate shapes The deformation is therefore constrained not only by position, but also by differential information. # Interior / exterior loss Surface constraints alone are not sufficient. We must also preserve which points are inside and outside the shape. # Landmark loss Given correspondences: $$ \mathcal{C} = \{ (x_0,x_1) \} $$ we enforce: $$ \phi((x_0,0),1) \approx x_1 $$ Landmarks provide semantic information when it is available. # Intermediate-time regularization Endpoint constraints alone do not control: $$ \mathcal{S}(t) \quad \text{for } 0 # Isometry We encourage: $$ J_{\psi_t}^T J_{\psi_t} \approx I $$ This promotes distance preservation. It helps prevent: - excessive stretching - spurious motion - geometric distortion # Volume preservation Local volume change is controlled by: $$ \det(J_{\psi_t}) $$ We penalize: $$ \log \det(J_{\psi_t}) $$ to encourage: $$ \det(J_{\psi_t}) \approx 1 $$ # Temporal regularization We penalize rapid temporal variations: $$ \mathcal{L}_T = \int \left\| \partial_t \psi_t(x) \right\|^2 \,dx\,dt $$ This produces smoother trajectories. # Shape interpolation No correspondences. No landmarks. Only two implicit shapes: $$ \mathcal{S}_0 \longrightarrow \mathcal{S}_1 $$ # Arbitrary shape interpolation
Example of continuous interpolation: $$ t=0 \rightarrow 1 $$ # Comparison with other methods We compare EFIS with: - Neural Flows - ADADIV - NISE - LipMLP # Higher genus shapes EFIS is not restricted to genus-zero objects.
The only fundamental restriction is that topology must be preserved. # Interpolation with landmarks Without semantic correspondences: > A mathematically valid deformation may not be semantically meaningful. For articulated shapes, landmarks provide the missing information. # FAUST: with and without landmarks Landmarks prevent unnatural limb motion. # Explicit mesh advection Because the trajectories are explicit: $$ x(t) = \phi((x_0,0),t) $$ we can directly advect mesh vertices. No remeshing is required at intermediate times. # Advected mesh For nearly isometric deformations, details are preserved directly on the mesh. # Pairwise-to-any morphing Suppose we have: $$ \mathcal{S}_1, \mathcal{S}_2, \dots, \mathcal{S}_N $$ and a canonical shape: $$ \mathcal{S}_0 $$ Instead of computing all pairwise deformations... # The key idea Compute only: $$ N $$ flows: $$ \mathcal{S}_i \longrightarrow \mathcal{S}_0 $$ Then obtain every pairwise deformation by composition. # Complexity Naively: $$ \frac{N(N+1)}{2} $$ pairwise morphings. With a canonical shape: $$ \boxed{N} $$ optimized flows. All other transformations are obtained by composition. # Pairwise-to-any results Here, a sphere is used as the canonical shape. # Choice of the canonical shape The canonical shape is important. A poor canonical shape can introduce undesirable intermediate deformations. # Shape editing Now we only have one shape: $$ \mathcal{S} $$ The target is specified through a small set of prescribed displacements: $$ (x_0,x_1) $$ # Shape editing results We compare with: - ARAP - NFGP - EFIS # Why use a flow for editing? A direct deformation gives only: $$ \mathcal{S}_0 \longrightarrow \mathcal{S}_1 $$ EFIS gives: $$ \boxed{ \mathcal{S}(t) \quad \forall t\in[0,1] } $$ The entire editing motion is available. # Continuous editing trajectory
# Analysis We evaluate: - Other flow architectures - Invertibility - Group law error - Architecture choices - Loss ablations - Other implicit representations # Comparison in 2D EFIS produces smoother temporal trajectories than Neural Flows. # Loss ablation Each loss has a distinct role: - D: endpoint position - N: normal consistency - S: inside / outside - T: temporal smoothness - I: isometry # Limitations ### Topology preservation A flow is invertible. Therefore, EFIS cannot: - create holes - remove handles - merge disconnected components - split a shape into multiple components The source and target must have compatible topology. # Other limitations - Network expressivity depends on architecture depth - Optimization remains computationally expensive - The choice of canonical shape affects pairwise-to-any morphing - Explicit trajectories are especially useful for interpolation, but less important for standard generative tasks # Explicit Flows for Implicit Surfaces We introduced a neural architecture that directly constructs: $$ \boxed{ \text{an exact mathematical flow} } $$ without numerical integration. # Contributions ### Explicit flow construction Forward and inverse evaluation at the same cost. ### Implicit shape deformation Intermediate shapes are available at arbitrary times. ### Geometry processing applications - Shape interpolation - Landmark-constrained morphing - Pairwise-to-any morphing - Shape editing # Take-home message Instead of learning: $$ \text{vector field} \rightarrow \text{ODE solver} \rightarrow \text{trajectory} $$ we directly learn: $$ \boxed{ (x,t) \longmapsto \phi(x,t) } $$ with guaranteed flow structure. # Thank you ### Explicit Flows for Implicit Surfaces Camille Buonomo Julie Digne Raphaëlle Chaine

## Abstract Shape deformation for morphing or editing purposes is a central challenge in Computer Graphics. While numerous methods exist, few allow for the explicit evaluation of the deformation at arbitrary times and locations without relying on intricate advection or interpolation schemes. We propose a method that provides an explicit expression of the deformation parameterized as a flow for continuously deforming implicitly defined shapes. Our approach leverages invertible neural networks to guarantee that the deformation is a valid flow while providing differential quantities useful for geometric regularization. We demonstrate applications to shape morphing with and without landmarks, shape editing, and pairwise-to-any morphing, where pairwise morphings to a canonical shape can be composed to obtain transformations between arbitrary pairs of shapes. ## Example

## Abstract Shape interpolation is a long standing challenge of geometry processing. As it is ill-posed, shape interpolation methods always work under some hypothesis such as semantic part matching or least displacement. Among such constraints, volume preservation is one of the traditional animation principles. In this paper we propose a method to interpolate between shapes in arbitrary poses favoring volume and topology preservation. To do so, we rely on a level set representation of the shape and its advection by a velocity field through the level set equation, both shape representation and velocity fields being parameterized as neural networks. While divergence free velocity fields ensure volume and topology preservation, they are incompatible with the Eikonal constraint of signed distance functions. This leads us to introduce the notion of adaptive divergence velocity field, a construction compatible with the Eikonal equation with theoretical guarantee on the shape volume preservation. In the non constant volume setting, our method is still helpful to provide a natural morphing, by combining it with a parameterization of the volume change over time. We show experimentally that our method exhibits better volume preservation than other recent approaches, limits topological changes and preserves the structures of shapes better without landmark correspondences. ## BibTeX ```bibtex @article{Buonomo2025, author = {Buonomo, Camille and Digne, Julie and Chaine, Raphaëlle}, title = {Volume Preserving Neural Shape Morphing}, journal = {Computer Graphics Forum}, volume = {44}, year = {2025}, doi = {10.1111/cgf.70196} } ``` ## Acknowledgements This work was partially funded by ANR-23- PEIA-0004 (PDE-AI).
